name: 'Toward Better Efficiency vs. Fidelity Tradeoffs in Web Archives' (Jingyuan Zhu, Huanchen Sun, Harsha V. Madhyastha; ACM IMC 2025, Madison WI, Oct 2025; DOI 10.1145/3730567.3764507). Part of a coherent research lineage from the same group: Jawa (OSDI 2022) -> Sprinter (NSDI 2024) -> this paper (IMC 2025) -> 'Detecting and Diagnosing Errors in Serving Archived Web Pages' (NSDI 2026).
kind: Research result (systems paper) proposing a resource-reuse technique for web-archive crawl infrastructure, not a library or standard. Directly relevant to this project as the most current academic treatment of the dynamic-browser-vs-static-crawl fidelity/cost tradeoff its own architecture must also navigate.
maturity: Research prototype presented at a top-tier venue (ACM IMC 2025); NSF-funded (Award 2403432); part of an actively continuing research program from the same authors (a 2026 NSDI follow-up on error detection in archived pages already exists), indicating the line of work is maturing rather than one-off. Not confirmed as adopted by a production archive (e.g. Internet Archive, Conifer/Webrecorder) at this time.
license: Not applicable in the software-license sense -- this is a paper, not a released tool; no separate open-source artifact release was confirmed from available (non-paywalled) sources in this pass.
keeps_and_discards: The system's core move: it KEEPS the fidelity of a full browser-based dynamic crawl (which captures all page resources including those only fetched when scripts execute) while DISCARDING most of the compute cost of running a browser on every page, by (a) sharing crawled resources across different pages and across repeated crawls of the SAME page over time, and (b) using a small number of dynamic (browser) crawls to learn which additional resources a static (browserless) crawl of a similar/same page needs to fetch WITHOUT executing scripts, then augmenting the static crawl's resource-fetch list accordingly.
structure_preserved: Not primarily a content-extraction structural question -- the concern is RESOURCE completeness (whether all page dependencies: scripts, stylesheets, images, XHR/fetch-triggered assets are captured), not DOM nesting/order fidelity within extracted text. The paper's fidelity unit of measure appears to be page-serving correctness under replay (whether the archived page renders/loads correctly later), inherited from the same group's prior Sprinter/Jawa work, though the exact operational fidelity metric (visual diff vs. resource-set diff vs. rendering-error detection) could not be independently confirmed from primary-source text in this pass (ACM DL and USENIX PDFs both returned 403; see uncertain).
interactive_elements: Not the paper's focus -- it addresses resource fetching/serving fidelity, not interactive-control capture or replay interactivity.
interactive_state_fidelity: Not addressed -- orthogonal to this paper's resource-reuse contribution.
layout_awareness: Not directly addressed in available material, though the broader Sprinter/Jawa lineage's notion of 'high fidelity' crawling is understood (from the group's stated research problem) to mean a REPLAYED page visually and functionally resembles the live page, which implicitly depends on layout-affecting resources (CSS, fonts, images) being present -- but the mechanism itself operates at the resource-fetch level, not by reading rendered geometry.
javascript_required: This is the paper's central axis. Dynamic (browser-based) crawlers execute JavaScript and thereby discover script-triggered resource fetches; static (browserless) crawlers do NOT execute scripts and therefore MISS such resources by default -- the paper's contribution is specifically a technique to let a static crawl fetch those same resources WITHOUT executing the scripts that would normally trigger them, by reusing knowledge from a prior dynamic crawl.
evaluation_method: Not independently confirmed in full from primary-source text (paywalled). Based on the confirmed abstract and consistent framing across the group's publication lineage, the method is comparative: dynamic-crawl-served fidelity is the ground truth/reference, and the paper measures how close statically-served (augmented) pages come to that reference across an evaluation corpus, reporting the fraction of statically-served pages achieving fidelity parity with dynamic crawling.
corpus_size_and_origins: Not confirmed from available (non-paywalled) sources -- exact page/site counts and origin diversity for this specific paper's evaluation corpus could not be extracted (ACM DL 403, USENIX-hosted companion PDFs 403). This is a genuine gap in this research pass, flagged in `uncertain` below rather than guessed.
reported_precision_recall: The paper's headline quantitative result, confirmed from multiple independent search-summary sources: 'if 8.9% of page crawls use a browser, an archive can serve roughly 99% of the remaining statically crawled pages without any loss in fidelity, up from 55% without their techniques.' Read carefully: the DENOMINATOR is 'remaining statically crawled pages' (i.e. the 91.1% not dynamically crawled); the BASELINE (no resource-reuse technique) achieves only 55% fidelity-parity on those statically served pages even with the SAME 8.9% dynamic-crawl budget, while the paper's resource-reuse technique lifts that to ~99% -- a roughly 44-percentage-point improvement at fixed dynamic-crawl budget, which is the paper's efficiency-vs-fidelity contribution in one sentence.
independent_oracle: The dynamic (full browser) crawl itself serves as the reference/oracle against which static-crawl-with-reuse fidelity is measured -- this is an INTERNALLY consistent oracle (both the training signal and the evaluation reference derive from the same class of dynamic crawls) rather than an externally independent one (e.g. a human visually confirming the page renders correctly), a limitation shared with most systems-style fidelity papers in this space.
evidence_independence: Independent academic authorship (University of Michigan / USC group), NSF-funded, not affiliated with or funded by a commercial web-archiving vendor as far as confirmed -- a genuinely independent research result, consistent with the group's broader publication record (Jawa, Sprinter, FABLE, link-rot characterization studies) which is not vendor-tied.
page_archetype_coverage: Not confirmed from available sources whether the evaluation corpus was stratified by page archetype (article/forum/product/etc.) in the WCXB sense -- likely NOT, since this line of work's unit of concern is resource/script-dependency structure rather than content-genre structure, but this could not be independently verified.
script_and_locale_behaviour: Not addressed in available material -- the paper's concern is JavaScript EXECUTION vs. non-execution as a binary resource-discovery mechanism, not script/locale (language) diversity in the CleanEval/multilingual-study sense.
leaks_outward: Not directly addressed as a privacy concern in available material -- this is a crawl-infrastructure efficiency paper, not a privacy paper. Indirectly relevant: reusing resources fetched during ONE page's dynamic crawl to serve requests for OTHER pages/times raises a latent question (not discussed in the confirmed abstract) about whether resource reuse could ever leak page-specific dynamic content (e.g. a personalized script response) into an unrelated page's served archive -- a risk this project should independently consider if adopting the technique, since the paper's own text on this was not accessible to confirm either way.
mechanism_detectability: Not applicable -- this is archive-serving infrastructure, not a live-page capture technique whose detectability by the origin site matters; the mechanism operates on already-crawled/archived data.
countermeasures: Not applicable -- no adversarial-detection concern in this paper's scope.
measured_fidelity_cost: The paper's OWN measured cost/benefit tradeoff (see reported_precision_recall): at a fixed 8.9% dynamic-crawl fraction, resource reuse costs essentially nothing extra in compute (it reuses already-fetched resources) while lifting fidelity from 55% to ~99% -- i.e. the measured 'cost' of the fidelity-hardening technique is near-zero marginal compute, which is the paper's whole selling point. Exact compute-overhead numbers (e.g. absolute CPU/memory cost of a browser-based crawl vs. static crawl) were not independently confirmed from primary-source text in this pass.
gate_state_at_capture: Not addressed in available material -- the paper's concern is resource-fetch completeness, not authentication/consent/paywall state; whether dynamic crawls used for resource-reuse training were behind any gate is not confirmed.
determinism: Not directly addressed; implicitly relevant because resource reuse assumes a STATIC (browser-triggered) resource fetch will produce the SAME resource identity/content when later fetched without a browser -- which depends on the target server's own determinism (e.g. no per-request randomized asset URLs), a dependency the paper's contribution silently relies on but which is not itself under the archive's control.
determinism_across_versions: Not addressed -- no discussion found of whether resource-reuse mappings need to be re-learned as target sites update their scripts/resources over time (this is closely related to the 'time-to-staleness' question flagged uncertain below, and is the more general concern the group's own NSDI 2026 follow-up paper on 'Detecting and Diagnosing Errors in Serving Archived Web Pages' appears to specifically address, suggesting the IMC 2025 paper itself may leave this gap for future work).
reproducibility: Not confirmed whether code/data are released; the paper's methodology (resource sharing across pages/time, dynamic-crawl-informed static-crawl augmentation) is described precisely enough in the abstract to be independently reimplemented in principle, but exact reproduction of the 8.9%/99%/55% figures would require the same evaluation corpus, which was not confirmed as released.
failure_modes: Not directly enumerated in available material. The single most obvious latent failure mode, inferable from the mechanism itself even without the full paper text: STALENESS -- a resource fetched during one dynamic crawl and reused to augment a LATER static crawl of the same or a similar page could silently serve an outdated or mismatched resource if the origin site has since changed its script behavior or resource URLs, and whether/how the paper detects or bounds this risk was not confirmed (flagged uncertain).
failure_visibility: Not confirmed from available material whether the system reports resource-reuse mismatches loudly or serves stale/wrong resources silently -- this is exactly the kind of gap this project's own no-mocks / failure_visibility commitments would flag as needing resolution before adoption, and is unresolved from the sources available in this pass.
scale_limits: The paper's entire framing IS a scale-limit argument: full dynamic (browser) crawling of every page 'incurs high compute overheads,' motivating the whole resource-reuse technique as a way to keep dynamic-crawl-fraction low (8.9% in their headline result) while still achieving near-total fidelity across the rest of the corpus -- i.e. the paper's contribution is explicitly a way to push the ELSE-LINEAR compute-cost curve of full-fidelity crawling toward sublinear by amortizing dynamic-crawl cost across many static crawls.
delta_cost_model: Closely analogous to this project's own O(delta) interest, though framed differently: the paper's resource-reuse mechanism is itself a form of amortized/delta-based cost model -- once a dynamic crawl has 'paid' the full cost for a page or resource pattern, SUBSEQUENT crawls of the same or related pages pay a much smaller marginal (static-crawl-plus-reuse) cost rather than re-paying the full dynamic-crawl cost each time. This is conceptually the same amortization principle the project's own ingest-cost concerns (582/840/1539ms at 136/250/500 pages) would want to validate against -- if the underlying cost model is NOT actually falling to near-static-crawl-cost after the first dynamic pass, the amortization claim would not hold, but this project's own measured superlinear ingest-cost growth suggests amortization is NOT automatically achieved by resource-sharing alone and needs its own verification.
reanchoring_stability: Not applicable in the DOM re-anchoring sense -- the paper's 'reuse' concept operates over crawled RESOURCES (files fetched by URL/hash), not over DOM element identity across page mutations; a related but distinct notion of identity stability (resource-URL/content-hash stability over time) is implicit but not the same mechanism this project's own reanchoring_stability field targets.
adversarial_exposure: Not addressed -- no adversarial/injection concern discussed in available material for this paper.
provenance_carrying: Not addressed directly, though implicitly relevant: reusing a resource fetched during crawl A to serve a request originating from crawl/page B means the served resource's PROVENANCE (which crawl, which page, what capture time it actually came from) diverges from the naive assumption that a page's resources were all fetched at that page's own capture time -- whether the system tracks and exposes this provenance distinction (versus silently presenting reused resources as if freshly fetched for the requesting page) was not confirmed from available sources, and is directly relevant to this project's own provenance_carrying commitment if any similar reuse technique were considered.
roundtrip_safety: Not applicable -- no serialize/parse/reparse concept in this paper's scope.
token_budget_and_ordering: Not applicable -- this is web-archive infrastructure, not an SLM-facing representation.
representation_cost: Not applicable in the token sense; the paper's analogous concept is COMPUTE cost (browser CPU/memory overhead) rather than token cost, and exact absolute overhead numbers were not confirmed from available sources.
what_could_be_adopted: The AMORTIZATION PRINCIPLE is the one directly transferable idea, decoupled from the paper's specific archive-serving use case: use a small fraction of full-fidelity (browser-executed, script-aware) captures to learn which additional resources/behaviors a lighter-weight capture of similar pages needs, rather than paying full browser-execution cost on every single ingest. For THIS project specifically, given the O(delta) open question about superlinear ingest-cost growth (582->840->1539ms at 136/250/500 pages, cProfile attributing only ~6%), the paper's framing suggests investigating whether the unattributed ~94% of cost growth resembles a similar 'repeatedly re-paying full-fidelity cost per page' pattern that could, in principle, be amortized the same way -- though this project's own architecture (a live browser-based sensor reading real DOM state, not a static/dynamic crawl dichotomy) is different enough that the SPECIFIC resource-reuse mechanism may not transfer directly; only the amortization PRINCIPLE is confidently adoptable.
constraint_violation_ledger: structure_agnosticism: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- the paper's resource-reuse technique operates on resource URLs/fetch patterns, not on page-region classification; it introduces no heuristic naming of nav/article/result regions. no_layout_in_the_fold: ADOPTABLE AS-IS -- the mechanism concerns script-triggered resource FETCHING, not rendered geometry; no layout-reading is implied. o_delta: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AT THE PRINCIPLE LEVEL, WITH AN OPEN VERIFICATION QUESTION -- the amortized-cost idea is directly aligned with an O(delta) goal, but this project would need to independently verify the analogous amortization actually explains its OWN superlinear ingest-cost growth before treating the transfer as validated; the paper's own 8.9%-dynamic-crawl-budget result does not by itself prove this project's specific bottleneck is resource-refetch-shaped. no_mocks: ADOPTABLE AS-IS AND ALIGNED -- the paper's method operates on real browser crawls and real resource fetches throughout, with no stubbing; the only unresolved risk (staleness of reused resources silently serving outdated content) is a FIDELITY risk, not a mocks/stub risk, and is flagged separately. closed_shadow_roots_stay_closed: NOT APPLICABLE -- the paper does not address shadow-DOM capture; orthogonal to this constraint. OVERALL VERDICT: adoptable as-is at the AMORTIZATION-PRINCIPLE level (use a minority of full-fidelity passes to inform the bulk of lighter-weight passes), but the specific staleness/provenance risks this research pass could not resolve from primary sources (resource reuse potentially serving outdated content without visible failure) mean any direct implementation should be treated as adoptable in the actuator layer only until this project can independently confirm failure_visibility and reanchoring/staleness bounds for its own equivalent mechanism.
governance_signal_handling: Not addressed -- orthogonal to this paper's scope.
legal_basis_and_pii_posture: Not addressed in available material -- a web-archive infrastructure paper of this kind typically does not engage PII/lawful-basis questions directly, though any real archive built on this technique would inherit the same PII-retention questions as web archiving generally (not specific to this paper's contribution).
uncertain: corpus_size_and_origins (could not be extracted -- both ACM Digital Library and USENIX-hosted PDF links returned HTTP 403 in this research pass; only the confirmed abstract and search-engine summaries were accessible)

evaluation_method / exact fidelity metric definition (visual diff vs. resource-set diff vs. automated rendering-error detection was not confirmed from primary-source text; inferred as resource-completeness-based from the group's consistent framing across Jawa/Sprinter but not independently verified for THIS specific paper)
failure_modes and failure_visibility (staleness risk of reused resources is a reasoned inference from the mechanism's design, not a confirmed statement from the paper itself)
measured_fidelity_cost absolute compute-overhead numbers for dynamic vs. static crawling (only the relative 8.9%/99%/55% figures were confirmed; absolute CPU/memory/time costs were not extracted)

Whether this paper's resource-reuse technique has any interaction with per-page personalization/session-specific dynamic content that could cause cross-page resource leakage was not addressed by the paper and is flagged as an open question this project should independently consider rather than assume resolved
